FINAL ANSWER (natural-language hypothesis)

Original papers in Experimental Economics are, on average, far longer than those in Psychology: the 18 original papers of the Experimental Economics replication project (project=='ee') average 28.00 pages (median 27.5), whereas the 95 unique original papers of the Psychology replication project RPP (project=='rpp', deduplicated by title from 97 rows) average 11.23 pages (median 9.0). This is a difference of about 16.8 pages — Experimental Economics papers are roughly 2.5× as long as Psychology papers in these replication datasets. The gap likely reflects field conventions (economics journals publish long full-length articles, psychology articles are much shorter), which is consistent with both projects testing the same kind of replication question but on very different publication formats.

Answer: Experimental Economics ≈ 28 pages per original paper; Psychology ≈ 11 pages per original paper (28.0 vs 11.2, a ~2.5× difference).

Sensitivity notes (one-liners, per your instruction):
- Excluding the 7 rpp rows flagged drop==True: Psychology mean 11.01 pages (n=88) — conclusion unchanged.
- Discipline-based Psychology variant (Social+Cognitive, unique titles across rpp/ml1/ml3, n=117): 11.16 pages — essentially the same, so the choice of definition does not drive the result.
